Carrion crows (Corvus corone) incubate their eggs at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that supports an average incubation period of 19 days [ab = 19 days]. This duration is typical for a corvid of this body mass and reflects the energetic constraints of maintaining such a stable internal microclimate within the nest, particularly during the variable spring weather of their temperate range. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings display a relatively low wet weight at birth, measured at 11.5 grams [Wwb = 11.5 grams]. This modest initial mass represents a significant parental investment in yolk and albumen, yet it is the starting point for a period of rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The synchronized emergence of the brood, which typically numbers between three and five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between three and five eggs per clutch], is a critical stage where the synchrony of hatching influences subsequent sibling competition and survival probabilities.

Once the chicks have hatched, their developmental trajectory under the sustained body temperature characteristic of active metabolic periods, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], proceeds through several well-defined milestones. The young reach the fledging stage, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, at 34 days after hatching [tx = 34 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many passerines and is followed by an extended phase of post-fledging parental care where the juveniles continue to beg for food while honing their foraging skills. The timing of fledging is a critical determinant of first-year survival, as individuals that leave the nest too early may lack sufficient flight muscle development, while those that delay may face increased predation risk within the nest. Consequently, the synchrony of this developmental event with peak food availability in the environment is a strong selective pressure.

The progression from fledgling to a reproductively viable adult involves a substantial period of physiological and behavioral maturation. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to produce gametes, is attained at 102 days after hatching [tp = 102 days after hatching] under the standard thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid achievement of sexual maturity compared to some larger corvids is offset by a considerable delay in actual first breeding. Individuals typically do not secure a territory and form a pair bond until much later, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 912 days since birth [tR = 912 days since birth] under the same thermal regime. This prolonged pre-breeding phase, often spanning several years, is common in long-lived birds with complex social structures, where experience and social dominance play key roles in reproductive success.

Adult body mass in the Carrion crow exhibits a distinct sexual size dimorphism, a common pattern among corvids. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing their asymptotic adult mass, averages 512 grams [Wwi = 512 grams]. Males, which are structurally larger and often more dominant in competitive interactions over food resources and nesting sites, attain a greater ultimate wet weight of 577 grams [Wwi = 577 grams]. This difference in body size has significant implications for the species' life history, influencing everything from daily energy budgets and metabolic rate to the size of prey items they can handle and their vulnerability to different predators. The higher mass of males may confer advantages in territorial defense, while the lighter female mass may be energetically advantageous during the demanding incubation and brooding periods. Population-level studies reveal that these masses are fairly stable across their European range, though slight local variations correlate with latitude and primary productivity.

Reproductive output in the Carrion crow is characterized by a relatively low annual rate, consistent with a K-selected life history strategy. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], although replacement clutches are laid if the first attempt fails early in the season. When combined with the typical clutch size of three to five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three to five eggs per clutch], this yields a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 4 to 5 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 4 to 5 offspring per year] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. While longevity data for Corvus corone itself are limited, information from the closely related Rook (Corvus frugilegus) provides a useful comparative benchmark; the Rook has a recorded maximum lifespan of approximately 7,008 days [am = approximately 7,008 days] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Given their similar life history traits and phylogenetic proximity, Carrion crows are presumed to possess a comparable potential longevity, though field studies often report much shorter realized lifespans due to anthropogenic mortality and environmental hazards.
